name: Gregory of Nazianzus

seo.title: St Gregory of Nazianzus: the Theologian, quotes and feast days
seo.description: Who Gregory of Nazianzus was, in plain words: Basil's best friend, the Theologian who gave up Constantinople, his feast days and his own words.

band.lede: Basil's best friend, and the poet and preacher the East still calls the Theologian.

who: Gregory was a bishop, preacher and poet from Cappadocia, in today's Turkey. He was Basil the Great's closest friend. His father made him a priest by force, and Basil made him a bishop against his will. In Constantinople, five sermons on the Trinity won him his name, the Theologian. Then he resigned and went home to write poems.

roles.name: Student
roles.line: Ten years at Athens, with Basil

lines: Sermons and speeches, some at his family's funerals
Five on the Trinity won him his name, the Theologian
206 of them about his life and his times
And 243 letters, by the same count
At the great council of 381, in Constantinople
He had chaired it for a time, then resigned as the city's bishop

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 329. Some say 325 or 330. At Arianzus, his father's estate near the small town of Nazianzus in Cappadocia, in **central Turkey** today.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: At Nazianzus. He studied at Caesarea in Cappadocia, Caesarea in Palestine and Alexandria, then about ten years at **Athens**.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: His father Gregory was bishop of Nazianzus. His mother Nonna had won his father to the faith. He had a sister, Gorgonia, and a brother, Caesarius, a doctor at the emperor's court. **All four are honoured as saints.**

facts.label: Died
facts.text: Probably in **389 or 390**, at Arianzus, where he was born. He had been ill for years.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: At Nazianzus. His relics later went to Constantinople and to Rome.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Gregory the Theologian**, in the Orthodox Church. **Gregory Nazianzen**, in the Catholic calendar. With Basil and John Chrysostom, one of the **Three Holy Hierarchs**.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans. Lutherans remember him too. For Catholics he is a **Doctor of the Church**.

facts.label: Patron of
facts.text: Poets, students, teachers and orthodoxy, says Britannica.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: In Eastern art, a bishop with a high forehead and a grey beard. He wears a white stole marked with crosses and holds a Gospel book. He is often shown with Basil and John Chrysostom.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Sermons, letters and poems. No Bible commentaries.

Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod**, with Basil and Gregory of Nyssa.
**Episcopal Church**. Also his day in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**.
In the **1916 Roman Martyrology**: his body moved into a chapel of St Peter's in Rome.

The **Three Holy Hierarchs**, with Basil and John Chrysostom.

feasts.note: The Orthodox keep 25 January, the day he died. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later by today's calendar, so 25 January falls on 7 February and 30 January on 12 February. Why 30 January? The OCA tells that in 1084 the three hierarchs appeared in a vision to John, bishop of Euchaita. They said they were equal before God, and asked for one feast together.

traits.title: a teasing wit
traits.text: He mocked Basil's beloved hermitage in Pontus as “your mousehole with the stately names of Abode of Thought, Monastery, School”. After a page of teasing he ended: “This is perhaps too long for a letter, but it is too short for a comedy.”

traits.title: fond of quiet
traits.text: Basil called him lazy for not taking up Sasima. Gregory wrote back: “My greatest business always is to keep free from business.” If everyone did the same, he added, the churches would have no troubles.

traits.title: quick to tears
traits.text: At his brother's funeral he had promised not to grieve too much. Soon he broke off: “how can I recall those days without my tears showing that, contrary to my promises, my feelings have overcome my philosophic restraint?” Remembering Athens with Basil, he stopped again: “Oh! how can I mention these things without tears.”

traits.title: a joke for a pupil
traits.text: Jerome once asked him to explain a hard phrase in Luke, the “second-first Sabbath”. Gregory put him off with a joke. He would explain it in church, he said, and then: “when all the people applaud me, you will be forced against your will to know what you do not know at all.”

traits.title: no avenger
traits.text: When a mob stoned his people in Constantinople, a friend wanted to take them to court. Gregory wrote to him that it is “far greater and more Godlike, to bear with injuries”. After Julian's persecution he told Christians: “Let us conquer those that have oppressed us, with clemency”.

cite.text: Letter 77, to Theodore; Oration 5, section 37, tr. C. W. King

traits.title: slow to heal
traits.text: Basil had used him to hold Sasima, and it hurt. Years later, in his speech in Basil's memory, he still called it “a cause of pain which even time has not obliterated”.

said.lede: Three who wrote of him: his pupil Jerome, the historian Socrates, and Pope Gregory the Great two centuries later.

quotes.q: Gregory, bishop of Nazianzen, a most eloquent man, and my instructor in the Scriptures
quotes.who: Jerome, who studied with him in Constantinople

quotes.q: Gregory, who far excelled in eloquence and piety all those of the age in which he lived
quotes.who: Socrates, a church historian writing in the next century

quotes.q: For, as long before us Gregory Nazianzen of reverend memory has taught, one and the same exhortation does not suit all
quotes.who: St Gregory the Great, about 590, opening the part of his Pastoral Rule that our personality test is built on

moments.title: The storm
moments.text: He sailed from Alexandria for Athens in November, out of season. Near Cyprus a great storm hit. The water tanks burst, and the ship would not answer the helm. He was not yet baptised, and that was his worst fear: “While we were all in fear of a common death, spiritual death was what I was most afraid of”. He prayed, and the crew prayed with him. He vowed himself to God. They reached Rhodes, and he kept his vow.

cite.text: Oration 18, on his father, section 31; the 1894 editors' life

moments.title: One soul in two bodies
moments.text: At Athens he met Basil again, and they became inseparable. They knew only two roads, one to church and one to their teachers. “We seemed to have one soul, inhabiting two bodies.” Among the students was the future emperor Julian. Gregory says he saw trouble in him even then, and cried out: “What an evil the Roman world is breeding!”

cite.text: Oration 43, on Basil, sections 20 and 21; Oration 5, section 24, tr. C. W. King

moments.title: Made a priest by force
moments.text: His old father and the people made him a priest against his will. He ran off to Basil in Pontus. By Easter he was back, and in his first sermon he forgave “the noble tyranny which I have suffered”. Then he wrote a long defence of why he had run. Guiding people, he wrote, is “the art of arts and science of sciences”.

moments.title: A bishop against his will
moments.text: Basil, now an archbishop, was fighting a rival bishop over a newly split province. To hold the border he made Gregory bishop of Sasima, a poor village there. Gregory never took it up. He wrote to Basil: “Give me before all things quiet. Why should I fight for sucking pigs and fowls, and those not my own, as though for souls and canons?” Their friendship never fully healed.

moments.title: His father's helper
moments.text: He stayed at Nazianzus to help his old father, the bishop. He had already buried his brother Caesarius and his sister Gorgonia. In 374 his father died too. Gregory preached at each of their funerals, and in those speeches he tells his family's wonders.

moments.title: The Anastasia
moments.text: The city's churches were in Arian hands. Gregory came to lead the small Nicene flock, and preached in a relative's house. He named it Anastasia, “Resurrection”. There he gave the five sermons on the Trinity that won him his name. At Easter a mob burst in during the baptisms and threw stones. Someone was killed.

cite.text: The 1894 editors' life; Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910; Gibbon, chapter 27

moments.title: A rival by night
moments.text: Gregory was taken in by an adventurer named Maximus, and praised him in public. Then, while Gregory lay ill, some bishops from Egypt made Maximus bishop in secret, at night. In the morning the people drove them out. That November the new emperor, Theodosius, took the churches from the Arians and led Gregory into the great church himself.

moments.title: The farewell
moments.text: At the great council of 381 he took the chair when its first president died. But the bishops shouted down his plan for peace at Antioch. He later said they sounded like a flock of jackdaws. Bishops who came late said his move from Sasima broke the church's rules. He resigned rather than fight, and asked in his farewell: “give me my desert, my country life, and my God, Whom alone I may have to please, and shall please by my simple life.”

moments.title: Home to the garden
moments.text: He handed Nazianzus to his cousin Eulalius and went home to the family estate. He wrote poems beside a spring, near a shady walk he loved. He wrote letters against Apollinarius, who taught that Christ had no human mind. One year he kept all of Lent in silence.

words.note: Gregory's own words, from his sermons and letters, in the 1894 translation by Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow.

feature.q: Farewell, O Trinity, my meditation, and my glory.
feature.ctx: Near the end of the speech in which he resigned. He had just said goodbye to his church, the city, East and West, and the angels. In Greek, {el|Χαῖρέ μοι, ὦ Τριὰς, τὸ ἐμὸν μελέτημα καὶ καλλώπισμα}.

quotes.q: For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.
quotes.who: Against Apollinarius, who taught that Christ had no human mind.

quotes.q: Christ is born, glorify ye Him. Christ from heaven, go ye out to meet Him. Christ on earth; be ye exalted.
quotes.who: The opening of his Christmas sermon. St Cosmas later set it in a Christmas hymn, and the Byzantine Christmas greeting, *Christ is born! Glorify Him!*, comes from it.

cite.text: Oration 38, on Christmas, section 1; Byzantine Catholic Archeparchy of Pittsburgh

quotes.q: Let us become like Christ, since Christ became like us. Let us become God's for His sake, since He for ours became Man.
quotes.who: His first sermon as a priest, Easter 362.

quotes.q: No sooner do I conceive of the One than I am illumined by the Splendour of the Three; no sooner do I distinguish Them than I am carried back to the One.
quotes.who: On the Trinity, in his sermon on baptism.

quotes.q: If a stranger fall at your feet, homeless and a foreigner, welcome in him Him Who for your sake was a stranger
quotes.who: In the same sermon, on how the baptised should live.

quotes.q: For they seek not for priests, but for orators, not for stewards of souls, but for treasurers of money, not for pure offerers of the sacrifice, but for powerful patrons.
quotes.who: On what many in the great city wanted in a bishop, in his farewell.

myths.truth: Close to his words, but only half of them. It is a shorter translation of the first half of a line in his letter to Cledonius. The 1894 translation reads “For that which He has not assumed He has not healed”, and the line goes on: “but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.”

myths.claim: Remember God more often than you breathe.
myths.truth: A loose paraphrase. He wrote that “we ought to think of God even more often than we draw our breath; and if the expression is permissible, we ought to do nothing else.” He said it while warning that not everyone should argue about God at every time.

myths.claim: As a fish cannot swim without water, and a bird cannot fly without air, so a Christian cannot advance a single step without Christ.
myths.truth: Shared widely as his. It comes from the introduction to the 1894 translation, which takes it from a writer it names only as Mr Crake. Neither names a work of Gregory's. It is not in any of his sermons or letters in that translation.

That was Basil. Gregory was made bishop of Sasima, where he never served, helped his father at Nazianzus, and led the church of Constantinople from 379 to 381. The Collins dictionary makes this mistake.

myths.claim: He and Gregory of Nyssa were brothers.
myths.truth: Gregory of Nyssa was Basil's younger brother. Gregory of Nazianzus was their friend.

cite.text: Letters to Gregory of Nyssa, with the editors' note

myths.claim: The Hymn to God, *O Thou beyond all things*, is his.
myths.truth: Some authors give it to him. A 2018 study says it was “most probably composed by a Christian Neoplatonist such as Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite”.

stood.lede: Each line is his own. The line on laughter is his praise of Basil's wit. The line on the poor is our translation from his Greek.

circle.name: Basil the Great
circle.text: His closest friend from their student days. As archbishop, Basil made him bishop of Sasima against his will, and the friendship never fully healed. Years later Gregory gave the great speech in his memory.

circle.name: Gregory the Elder
circle.text: His father, bishop of Nazianzus. He made his son a priest by force, and Gregory served beside him until he died in 374.

circle.name: Nonna
circle.text: His mother. She won his father to the faith. Gregory said “it was on her part a great undertaking to promise me to God before my birth”.

circle.name: Gorgonia and Caesarius
circle.text: His sister and brother. Caesarius was a doctor at the emperor's court. Gregory preached at both their funerals.

circle.name: Gregory of Nyssa
circle.text: Basil's younger brother. Gregory scolded him for choosing “to be called a Professor of Rhetoric rather than of Christianity”. When Basil died, he wrote to him in grief.

circle.name: Jerome
circle.text: Studied the Scriptures with him in Constantinople, and called him “my teacher”.

cite.text: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 117; Letter 52

circle.name: Julian the Apostate
circle.text: A fellow student at Athens, later the emperor who tried to bring back the old gods. After Julian died, Gregory attacked him in two fierce speeches.

circle.name: Maximus the Cynic
circle.text: The adventurer who won Gregory's trust, then had himself made bishop of Constantinople in secret, in Gregory's place.

circle.name: Nectarius
circle.text: A leading official, not yet baptised, chosen bishop of Constantinople when Gregory resigned. Gregory wrote to him kindly afterwards.

death.big: He died at Arianzus, where he was born, probably in 389 or 390. He had been ill for years.
paras: No account of his death survives. The Orthodox keep 25 January as the day he died.
His will left everything he owned to a deacon named Gregory for life, and after that to the poor of Nazianzus. His 1894 editors think it is probably genuine.

later.title: Where his relics went
later.text: He was buried at Nazianzus. In 950 his relics were taken to the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople, and part of them later reached Rome. Pope Gregory XIII moved them into a chapel of St Peter's. In 2004 Pope John Paul II gave relics of Gregory and of John Chrysostom back to the Patriarch of Constantinople. His head is kept at Vatopedi Monastery on Mount Athos, says the OCA.

cite.text: OCA; The Roman Martyrology (1916), 11 June; John Paul II, 27 November 2004

items.q: My children, keep, I pray you, that which is committed to your trust. Remember my stonings.
items.ctx: Near the very end of his farewell in 381. No words from his deathbed survive.

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans count him a saint, and Lutherans remember him too. His own generation already called him a saint, says the OCA.

churches.note: A Doctor of the Church. 2 January, with Basil
Church of England 2 January, Episcopal Church 9 May

paras: The Roman Martyrology of 1916 remembered him on 9 May. The historian Edward Gibbon, writing in 1781, praised him for something else.

quotes.q: At Nazianzus, the birthday of St. Gregory, bishop and doctor of the church, surnamed the Theologian, because of his remarkable knowledge of divinity. At Constantinople, he restored the Catholic faith, which was fast waning, and repressed the rising heresies.
quotes.who: The Roman Martyrology, 1916 edition, for 9 May

quotes.q: The title of Saint has been added to his name: but the tenderness of his heart, and the elegance of his genius, reflect a more pleasing lustre on the memory of Gregory Nazianzen.

cite.text: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, chapter 27

prayer.intro: He wrote this prayer to end his funeral speech for his brother Caesarius. He prays for his brother, and for those still living.
prayer.q: O Lord and Maker of all things, and specially of this our frame! O God and Father and Pilot of men who are Thine! O Lord of life and death! O Judge and Benefactor of our souls! O Maker and Transformer in due time of all things by Thy designing Word, according to the knowledge of the depth of Thy wisdom and providence! do Thou now receive Cæsarius, the firstfruits of our pilgrimage; and if he who was last is first, we bow before Thy Word, by which the universe is ruled; yet do Thou receive us also afterwards, in a time when Thou mayest be found, having ordered us in the flesh as long as is for our profit; yea, receive us, prepared and not troubled by Thy fear, not departing from Thee in our last day, nor violently borne away from things here, like souls fond of the world and the flesh, but filled with eagerness for that blessed and enduring life which is in Christ Jesus, our Lord, to Whom be glory, world without end. Amen.

cite.text: Oration 7, on his brother Caesarius, section 24

extras.title: Wonders he told
extras.lede: In these stories Gregory works no wonder himself. He tells them in his funeral speeches: wonders in his own family, and at sea when he was young.

items.title: His father at Easter
items.text: His old father lay dying of a fever. His mouth was so ulcered that he could hardly swallow water, and the doctors could do nothing. On Easter night the people prayed for him in church. At the hour of the mysteries he stirred. He called a servant to bring his clothes and hold him up. There, far from the altar, he celebrated the mysteries in the few words his strength allowed. Then he went back to bed, ate a little and slept. A week later he led the service in church.
items.quote: he was raised up by Him Who quickeneth the dead, and by the holy night

cite.text: Oration 18, on his father, sections 28 and 29

items.title: Loaves in a dream
items.text: His mother Nonna could not eat, and for days her life was in danger. She dreamed that Gregory came to her at night with a basket of pure white loaves. He blessed them and fed her. In the morning she was brighter. When he asked how she had slept, she said:
items.quote: My child, you most readily and kindly fed me, and then you ask how I am. I am very well and at ease.

items.title: Gorgonia at the altar
items.text: His sister Gorgonia had a dangerous illness with a constant fever. The doctors could do nothing. One night she went to the altar, laid her head on it, and said she would not let go until she was healed. Then she rubbed over her body what she had kept in her hand of the Sacrament, mixed with her tears. She told no one while she lived. Gregory told it at her funeral.
items.quote: O the wonder, she went away feeling at once that she was saved

cite.text: Oration 8, on his sister Gorgonia, sections 17 and 18

items.title: A vision in the storm
items.text: In the storm at sea, his parents at home learned of his danger in a dream, and prayed. Gregory dreamed he was holding a Fury, a sign of danger. A boy on board, who loved him, saw something else. Then the sea began to calm.
items.quote: thought he saw my mother walk upon the sea, and seize and drag the ship to land with no great exertion

items.title: Light at the font
items.text: His father was baptised as a grown man. As he came up out of the water, a light shone around him. Some saw it and said nothing for a time, each thinking he alone had seen it. The bishop who baptised him cried out that he was anointing his own successor.
items.quote: there flashed around him a light and a glory

items.title: He knew some would doubt
items.text: Gregory answered doubt himself. Of Gorgonia he said: “Great though these things be, they are not untrue.” Of his father he told his hearers: “though you, my hearers, may shudder, do not disbelieve”. And he told the light at the font “to the ears of the faithful, for to profane minds nothing that is good is trustworthy.”

extras.title: Hard questions
extras.lede: Gregory has critics. Here are the hard questions, in his own words and in theirs.

items.title: His speeches against Julian
items.text: After the emperor Julian died, Gregory attacked him in two long speeches. They paint what his 1894 editors call “a very dark picture” of Julian. The historian Gibbon wrote that Julian was “overwhelmed with a torrent of pious invectives, of which the signal was given by the sonorous trumpet of Gregory Nazianzen”. Yet in the second speech Gregory told Christians to take no revenge on Julian's men:
items.quote: let us not do to them anything of all that they have done to us

cite.text: The 1894 editors; Gibbon, chapter 23; Oration 5, section 37, tr. C. W. King, 1888

items.title: Second marriages
items.text: He taught that a first marriage is the law, and he was hard on a third: “The first is law, the second is indulgence, the third is transgression, and anything beyond this is swinish”. In the same sermon he attacked laws that punished a wife's adultery but not a husband's:
items.quote: I do not accept this legislation; I do not approve this custom. They who made the Law were men, and therefore their legislation is hard on women

items.title: Hell, and mercy
items.text: He taught an unquenchable fire that is “eternal for the wicked”. But he added that “some may prefer even in this place to take a more merciful view of this fire, worthily of Him That chastises.” His translators note that this was not his own reading, “though he admits it to be tenable”. Elsewhere he says that those who refuse mercy to sinners who repent will perhaps be “baptized with Fire, in that last Baptism which is more painful and longer”.

items.title: Ambition, or humility?
items.text: Critics at the council said his move to Constantinople broke the rule against bishops changing sees. He resigned rather than fight. The historian Gibbon was not sure which it was: “The pride, or the humility, of Gregory prompted him to decline a contest which might have been imputed to ambition and avarice”. Gregory said in his farewell:
items.quote: I am weary of being charged with my gentleness.

tidbits.text: In 382 he was called to another council of bishops, and refused to go. He had never known any good come of one, he said.

A relative, Nicobulus, asked him for a book of his letters. Gregory put Basil's letters first and his own second. He had always ranked Basil above himself, he explained, and he hoped the two of them would always be paired.

He had three rules for a good letter. Make it as long as the matter needs, no longer and no shorter. Write plainly, the way people talk. Add charm with a proverb or a joke, but sparingly, as purple is used in cloth.
